units.translation: Κισσία [Cissia] is a region of Susiana which was called Κισσίη γῆ [Cissian land] or χώρη [country] by Herodotus 5,49 and 52. 6, 19. The inhabitants are called Κίσσιοι [Cissians] by Strabo 15 p. 728 λέγονται δὲ καὶ Κίσσιοι οἱ Σούσιοι · φησὶ δὲ καὶ Αἰσχύλος [the Susians are also called Cissians; and Aeschylus also says] (fr. 279) that the mother of Memnon was Cissian.

Aeschylus distinguishes the Κισσίους [Cissians] from the Susians, where their city is mentioned, where Blomfield restored Κίσσιον [Cissium] for Κίσσινον [Cissinum], which had been introduced by a careless scribe because of the similarity of the adjective κίσσινος [of ivy], which means hederaceus [ivy-covered].
The correct spelling is preserved in M there, although here too it is corrupted into Κισσίνων [Cissinon] in some copies.
Those who left the citadel of Susa and Ecbatana and the ancient Cissian fortress and went forth
And the city of the Cissians will sing in response
By the laws of a Cissian wailing woman
the Susians are also called Cissians; and Aeschylus also says
the mother of Memnon as Cissian
Since otherwise, stranger, you go to Argos
Pillars (in the dual number) of heaven and earth, pressing on his shoulders

Thus Wakefield for κλαγγαίνεις [you ring], which is in M, just as ὀλισθαίνειν [to slip] and οἶδαίνειν [to swell] are not infrequently written in manuscripts for ὀλισθάνειν [to slip] and οἰδάνειν [to swell]. Correctly written in Sophocles fr. 782.

Thus H. L. Ahrens for κέκλαγεν [has rung], which Robortellus had changed to κέκραγεν [has cried]. On the perfect κέκλαγγα [I have rung] (whose subjunctive is κεκλάγγω [I may ring] in Arist. Vesp. 929), which in epic is κέκληγα [I have rung], see Veitch p. 328.
And she, startled from sleep, has rung out
With midday clangings, like a serpent, he cries
With ill-omened clang you strike the lyre
And the high-born branch of olive
With these suppliants' hand-held, wool-wreathed branches
The branches indeed lie before you
And taking these branches quickly in your arms
Screaming great Ares from their hearts
And someone eagerly screaming victory songs to Zeus
The pipes screamed with their whirling reeds
I will scream a tearful lament
Another device against the storm; the prophet screamed

which is a Doric form for κληρίου [of the lot], as Pausanias 8, 35, 9 teaches: τὸ δὲ χωρίον τὸ ὑψηλὸν, ἐφ᾽ οὗ καὶ οἱ βωμοὶ Τεγεάταις εἰσὶν οἱ πολλοί, καλεῖται μὲν Διὸς κλαρίου, δῆλα δὲ ὡς ἐγένετο ή ἐπίκλησις τῷ θεῷ τοῦ κλήρου τῶν παί-δων εἵνεκα τῶν Ἀρκάδος [The high place, on which the many altars of the Tegeans are, is called of Zeus Clarius, and it is clear that the surname of the god came from the lot of the children of Arcas].
